clue.text: Nervous, following a convoluted course abounding in words

definitions.meaning: informal British sense: scared or jittery
describes a road or river that twists and bends
describes a speaker who is verbose and long-winded

explanation.surface: A jittery traveller on a twisting route who won't stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: A triple definition: three separate senses of one word, with no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Each phrase is a dictionary sense of the word: frightened (British slang), twisting, and long-winded.

clue.text: A head that strikes through to take the role of mother's lover

indicators.note: the strikers go through the middle of the tea-serving verb, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.words: to take the role of mother
parts.note: 'Shall I be mother?' is the British offer to serve the tea, so playing mother means to pour
a battering ram is the striking head that breaks down a door

explanation.surface: A battering-ram-like suitor muscles in to play the part of mum's boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shall I be mother?' is the British offer to serve the tea, so 'mother' is about the teapot, not a parent. The 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: an illicit or secret lover, typically of someone married.

clue.text: Hooked head's given pass into Congress

indicators.note: the pass is put into the word for congress, one piece inside the other

parts.note: sexual congress, so congress means sex
a col is a mountain pass

explanation.surface: A legislative leader with a hook for a head gets a bill passed in Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: Congress looks political but means sexual intercourse. This half of the hidden EXPRESS (with 17 Down) is one of the two papers 'gone bust'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scolex is a tapeworm's head, armed with hooks for gripping the gut wall.

clue.text: Miles:millilitres, in which there's one:one correspondence

indicators.note: says the unit letters hold the pair of ones within them

parts.note: m is the abbreviation for miles and ml for millilitres; the ratio supplies M and L
A and I each mean one

explanation.surface: A unit-conversion table that matches miles to millilitres one to one.
explanation.walkthrough: The colons dress the clue as a ratio sum; both 'one's are letters (A and I), and 'in which there's' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Post sent and received is correspondence, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Poor Isaac and Rebecca primarily need to breathe

indicators.note: poor shows the letters of Isaac are in a bad, disordered state
primarily asks for the first letter of Rebecca

explanation.surface: Biblical Isaac and Rebecca, short of breath, need some air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges ISAAC into AIRSA; 'primarily' adds the R that begins Rebecca.
explanation.definitionFit: An air sac is an organ birds and insects need in order to breathe.

clue.text: See 21
Analysing, for instance, 4 — if it bears info for bankers

indicators.note: to analyse is to break something down, so the letters are taken apart and rebuilt

parts.note: the solution to 4 Down, the word for post

explanation.surface: Analysing post as an example, if it carries information meant for bankers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link; the anagram pool is INSTANCE, the 4 Down answer MAIL and IF.
explanation.definitionFit: The FT is the pink City newspaper read by financiers for market news.

clue.text: See 7
See 14
'Junk' Indian meal nine individually cancelled after ordering?

indicators.note: each letter of the number word is struck out one at a time, not as a block
the meal's letters are rearranged first, then the cancelling is done

parts.note: the letters N, I, N, E to be removed

explanation.surface: A takeaway curry menu pushed through the door, dismissed as junk.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle INDIAN MEAL, remove N, I, N, E one by one, and ADMAIL is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Admail is Royal Mail's name for bulk advertising post, which recipients call junk mail.

clue.text: Dublin location to have a sly look around this month

indicators.note: the sly look goes around the month abbreviation

parts.note: to leer is to look slyly or lasciviously
inst., short for instant, means this month in old business letters

explanation.surface: Planning to snoop around Dublin sometime this month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inst.' (instant) is an old commercial abbreviation for this month; 'around' puts it inside LEER.
explanation.definitionFit: Dublin lies in the Irish province of that name, so the province is where Dublin is.

clue.text: Don't leave me this way, love — I subsequently laid into nearest

indicators.note: the pair is laid into the word for nearest, placed inside it
then, after the love is placed, the single letter I goes in too, as a second insertion

parts.note: next door is the nearest one
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A plea to a departing lover, quoting the disco song, followed by a lovers' quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid into' puts O and, 'subsequently', I inside NEXT at separate points. 'Don't Leave Me This Way' is a 1970s song title; read literally it is what a sign blocking the way out says.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign forbidding departure by that route effectively says you cannot leave this way.

clue.text: Not what you'd expect double helping of pasta to include!

definitions.text: Not what you'd expect double helping of pasta to include!

indicators.note: a double helping means the word pasta is written out twice in a row
the pair of pastas contains a five-letter run straddling the join, which is the word with its end letters brought round to the front

explanation.surface: A surprised diner finds something unexpected inside a double portion of pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: Write PASTAPASTA and read the run across the join: the same as moving the final TA of pasta to the front. As a whole, the clue observes that Spanish snacks are not what an Italian dish should contain.
explanation.definitionFit: Small Spanish bar snacks are the last thing an Italian pasta dish would contain.

clue.text: Old musical organ the enemy picked up for a competitor in the market

definitions.meaning: organ means a periodical; this was a British pop-music weekly of the 1950s-90s

definitions.text: the enemy picked up for a competitor in the market
definitions.meaning: 'the enemy' heard aloud is 'the NME', the New Musical Express, and this weekly was its rival

explanation.surface: An antique organ, captured from the enemy, offered for sale in the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' means a publication, not an instrument. The second half sounds out 'the NME', a rival music weekly.
explanation.definitionFit: This British music paper was a direct rival of the New Musical Express on the newsstands.

clue.text: Knackered pacesetter relinquishing lead for others …

indicators.note: British slang for worn out or broken, so the remaining letters are wrecked and rearranged
the leading letter of the word is given up

explanation.surface: An exhausted pacemaker gives up the lead to the other runners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relinquishing lead' drops the P, leaving ACESETTER; 'Knackered' rearranges it. The ellipsis just carries on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means additional unnamed things of the same kind, as 'and so on' does: the others.

clue.text: Top actor's beginning, but not end

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for beginning is left off

parts.note: a start is a beginning

explanation.surface: A leading actor's career: a promising start but no ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not end' drops the last letter of START; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading or celebrated performer is called the star of a show.

clue.text: Producer of Pibroch, or the Walford Gazette?

definitions.meaning: pibroch is classical bagpipe music, played by a bagpiper
Walford is the fictional East London borough of the TV soap EastEnders, whose locals' Cockney accent turns 'paper' into this word

explanation.surface: Asking who produces a bagpipe piece, or a local London newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap set in Walford; in its Cockney the local 'paper' sounds like a bagpipe player.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of bagpipes performs pibroch, and in Cockney speech the local news-sheet is pronounced the same way.

clue.text: Perhaps the foundation for smoothie hairdresser perking locks up

indicators.note: in a down clue the held letters read upward, from bottom to top
the phrase locks the letters inside it, holding a run across its two words

explanation.surface: A hairdresser with a smoothing product perks up a client's locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks' looks like hair but holds the letters; 'up' reads them backwards in this down entry. With 3 Down it completes EXPRESS, the second paper 'gone bust'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressé is freshly squeezed fruit juice, which could be the base of a blended drink, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Wide angle to some extent opening aperture

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A photographer's wide-angle lens with the aperture partly opened.
explanation.definitionFit: To open wide is to yawn open, as a chasm or a mouth does; the wide angle of the jaws.

clue.text: Caretaker has King and I translated in foreign language

indicators.note: one rearranged group sits inside the other
made foreign, the letters of that word are rearranged

parts.note: R, for Rex, is the abbreviation for king

indicators.note: translating changes the form of these letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A carer with a copy of The King and I translated into another tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The King and I' is the musical; here it splits into a king's letter plus two words. Both 'translated' and 'foreign' signal rearrangement, and 'in' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A protecting spirit who watches over a person is a heavenly caretaker.

clue.text: Boil? ____ quack!

definitions.meaning: to boil with rage, to be furious
fill the blank with two words and the line becomes advice to go and visit the doctor (quack is slang for a doctor), as you might for a boil

explanation.walkthrough: Split 3,3 the answer fills the gap to advise a trip to the quack, the doctor. With 21 Across it holds THE SUN, one paper 'gone bust'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fume with anger is to bubble over inside, the figurative sense of boiling.

clue.text: This swimmer FBI's clobbered with rifle-butt?

indicators.note: clobbered means battered, so the letters are knocked about and rearranged

parts.note: the letters F, B, I are removed from the battered pool

explanation.surface: FBI agents beat a swimmer with the butt of a rifle.
explanation.walkthrough: RIFLEBUTT rearranged and less F, B, I leaves the reptile; the question mark flags the odd construction.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea turtle is a reptile that swims, so it is this swimmer.

clue.text: Our sister American is back, wandering legendary path

indicators.note: the abbreviation for American is turned back to front
the letters stray from their order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A legendary pilgrim, sister to an American, back on a wandering mythical road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns US to SU; 'wandering' rearranges LEGENDARY PATH. 'Our' is the Daily Telegraph, where the puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekend edition is the Daily Telegraph's sister paper, so for this crossword it is our sister.

clue.text: Extremely young crossword compilers comfortably ensconced?

indicators.note: the setters are settled inside, placed within the snug home

parts.note: a nest is where one settles comfortably, the snug place
setters often refer to themselves collectively as we

explanation.surface: Young setters who have settled comfortably into the crossword world.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters traditionally write of themselves in the editorial plural; 'comfortably' points to a snug home and 'ensconced' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of new: the most recent, so the youngest of all.

clue.text: See 18
Allowed Roma's wingers to fix transfer system

parts.note: let means allowed

indicators.note: the wingers are the letters on the outside edges of the word

parts.note: to set is to fix firmly in place

explanation.surface: Roma's wide players were allowed to fix a transfer deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wingers' takes the outside letters of Roma; it reads like footballers at AS Roma.
explanation.definitionFit: Letraset is the brand of dry-transfer lettering sheets, a rub-down transfer system.

clue.text: Not our diminished ego

indicators.note: made smaller, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: the possessive of others rather than ourselves

explanation.surface: Someone else's ego, not ours, cut down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diminished' drops the last letter; the result is also the i, a UK newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The ego is the self, the 'I' that thinks, so the definite article with the pronoun names it.

clue.text: Debuts for Arsenal defenders in side finding progress difficult

indicators.note: the two initials go in the word for side

parts.note: a wing is a side of a building or a team

indicators.note: the debuts are the opening letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: Arsenal's debutant defenders struggle out on the flank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side' looks like a football team, but here it is a building's or team's flank; 'Debuts for' takes initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking through water is laborious, so it means making slow headway.

clue.text: National grid displays many such here, two having gone bust!

definitions.text: National grid displays many such here, two having gone bust!

parts.words: National grid displays many such here, two having gone bust!
parts.note: the national grid is this crossword, whose answers include many British titles; two are split across entries

explanation.walkthrough: 'National grid' suggests the power network but is the crossword. The two 'bust' titles are EXPRESS (3 Down and 17 Down) and THE SUN (19 and 21 Across).
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet Street titles printed every weekday are the general class this grid is full of.
